title: Overcoming immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer: a narrative review of related factors
author: Liliana Gutiérrez-Babativa; Nicolle Wagner-Gutiérrez; Leonardo Rojas; Jairo Zuluaga; Oscar Arrieta; Andrés F Cardona
text:
ABSTRACT
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for over 80% of lung cancer cases and is often diagnosed at advanced stages. Resistance to immunotherapy in NSCLC involves genetic mutations, tumor microenvironment (TME) characteristics, treatment history, and age-related factors. Despite increasing use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), resistance mechanisms remain poorly understood. Key genetic alterations associated with resistance include STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR mutations, particularly with low tumor mutational burden (TMB). The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, characterized by regulatory T cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, can hinder ICI efficacy. Metabolic alterations and deficient antigen presentation contribute to resistance. Prior treatments can alter the tumor microenvironment, affecting subsequent immunotherapy responses. Age-related factors, including immunosenescence, influence resistance, with older patients having higher TMB and more immunogenic microenvironments. Strategies to overcome resistance include combination therapies, biomarker-driven approaches, and targeting novel pathways. Combining ICIs with chemotherapy or radiation can enhance antitumor responses. Biomarker approaches, such as TMB and PD-L1 expression assessment, help tailor therapies. Exploring novel targets like RIG-I and STING pathways may provide additional solutions. Understanding these factors is crucial for developing personalized strategies to overcome immunotherapy resistance in NSCLC.
KEYWORDS: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), tumor mutational burden (TMB), immunotherapy resistance, genetic mutations, age-related factors, STK11, KEAP1, tumor microenvironment
1. Introduction
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common subtype of lung cancer, comprising approximately 85% of cases, and is often present at advanced stages [1]. The use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) and its ligand (PD-L1), has transformed NSCLC treatment, particularly in patients with high PD-L1 expression [2]. ICIs have improved the overall survival rates, with five-year survival reaching up to 40% in advanced-stage patients with favorable biomarker profiles [1,3]. Despite these advances, drug resistance remains a significant challenge. Both primary resistance, observed in 20–27% of patients at treatment initiation, and acquired resistance, occurring in over 60% of patients who initially respond, limit the long-term effectiveness of ICIs [4].
The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a pivotal role in immune resistance and comprises immunosuppressive cells such as tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) that inhibit T-cell activity [2,5]. Additionally, tumors can evade immune attack through upregulation of alternative immune checkpoints, such as LAG-3 and VISTA, further suppressing the T-cell response [6]. Complicating these immune evasion strategies are specific genetic mutations in NSCLC, such as those in the STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR genes, which create additional immunosuppressive conditions by reducing T-cell infiltration and altering the TME, particularly in patients with low tumor mutational burden (TMB) [4,7].
The primary and acquired resistance mechanisms differ substantially. Primary resistance often arises due to immune “cold” tumors with poor immune cell infiltration, whereas acquired resistance can result from adaptive changes in the tumor, including antigen presentation loss and enhanced checkpoint molecule expression [3,6]. This immune exclusion effect in the TME, driven by TAMs, fibroblasts, and extracellular matrix proteins, can create physical and biochemical barriers that prevent immune cells from effectively reaching tumor cells [2]. Understanding these mechanisms highlights the need for therapies that can reprogram the TME and counteract these resistance pathways.
While ICIs have shown broad success across various cancer types, NSCLC presents unique resistance challenges owing to these genetic and environmental influences. Consequently, recent therapeutic strategies are shifting toward combination therapies, integrating ICIs with agents such as chemotherapy and radiation to promote immunogenic cell death, enhance tumor antigen presentation, and increase immune system targeting of tumor cells [8]. However, current biomarker profiles, although partially predictive, remain limited. A deeper understanding of NSCLC resistance mechanisms is essential to develop and personalize effective treatment strategies.
This review aims to integrate emerging evidence on the interplay of tumor genetics, microenvironment, treatment history, and age-related immune alterations, which has not been comprehensively explored in prior reviews. It provides a multidimensional framework for understanding resistance and personalized immunotherapy strategies [9,10].
This review is based on a narrative synthesis of peer-reviewed articles published between January 2018 and October 2024. PubMed and Scopus databases were searched using the following keywords: “NSCLC,” “immunotherapy resistance,” “tumor microenvironment,” “PD-L1,” and “TMB.” Two authors (LG and NWG) independently screened and selected the relevant studies.
Although several recent reviews have explored the mechanisms underlying immunotherapy resistance in NSCLC, most have focused exclusively on genomic alterations or immune checkpoint biology. This review differs in its integrative approach, examining not only genetic drivers but also the tumor microenvironment, prior treatment history, and age-related immune changes, with a particular emphasis on older adults. By synthesizing evidence across these domains, we aim to present a multidimensional framework to guide more precise immunotherapy strategies. In doing so, this study addresses a critical gap in the current literature and has the potential to inform both personalized treatment decisions and future biomarker development.
Recent reviews by Xiang et al. [9] and Huang et al. [10] provide valuable insights into immune evasion and tumor dynamics; however, they do not offer the same degree of integration across clinical, biological, and age-related factors, which are essential for understanding the complexity of resistance in real-world NSCLC populations.
2. Factors associated with immunotherapy resistance
Several factors can contribute to resistance to immunotherapy in NSCLC, including genetic mutations in STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR, tumor microenvironment characteristics, prior treatment history, and age-related factors. Resistance to immunotherapy is multifactorial and involves genetic mutations, tumor microenvironment characteristics, treatment history, and age-related factors.
2.1. Genetic mutations
Patients with NSCLC who experience resistance to immunotherapy often present specific clinical and molecular profiles. Genetic mutations, tumor microenvironment characteristics, and treatment history are the key factors that contribute to resistance. Alterations in key genes, such as EGFR, ALK, and ROS1 are strongly associated with resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Patients harboring these mutations often exhibit primary resistance to ICIs. Notably, mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 have emerged as strong biomarkers of ICI resistance as they contribute to an immunosuppressive TME and reduce T-cell infiltration [11–13].
Older patients (≥65 years) tend to exhibit a higher tumor mutational burden (TMB) and more frequent mutations in genes such as EGFR and ERBB2 than younger patients (<50 years). These genetic differences can affect the efficacy of ICIs, as a higher TMB is generally associated with better responses to ICIs. At the same time, specific mutations, such as EGFR, are linked to resistance [12,14]. However, the presence of specific mutations, such as EGFR, STK11, and KEAP1, can lead to immune evasion and poor outcomes despite high TMB levels, suggesting that TMB alone may be insufficient as a predictive biomarker in this population [2,3,6].
Genetic variations, such as mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), serine/threonine kinase 11 (STK11), and kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1), significantly influence the response to immunotherapy in older patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly in the context of tumor mutational burden (TMB). These mutations often result in an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) that limits T-cell infiltration and activity, thus compromising ICI efficacy [4,8].
2.1.1. EGFR Mutations
EGFR mutations are frequently associated with primary resistance to ICIs as they can upregulate PD-L1 expression and disrupt antigen presentation, enabling immune evasion [4,15]. Alterations in EGFR are also linked to primary resistance to ICIs. However, high TMB can mitigate this resistance, leading to occasional durable responses [13]. EGFR mutations are also linked to resistance, although high TMB can mitigate this effect. While EGFR mutations are often linked with lower TMB, some less common EGFR variants, such as G719X, may show higher TMB and PD-L1 levels, potentially yielding better responses to ICIs than classic EGFR mutations [13,16]. However, patients with EGFR mutations tend to exhibit limited responses to ICIs, and these cases often require alternative or combination therapeutic approaches to overcome resistance.
EGFR mutations are also associated with lower TMB and reduced efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). However, some uncommon EGFR mutations, such as G719X, may result in higher TMB and PD-L1 expression, potentially leading to better responses to ICIs than classical EGFR mutations [17,18]. Overall, EGFR mutations contribute to an “immune cold” phenotype characterized by lower levels of immune cell infiltration, which can further inhibit the response to ICIs [8].
2.1.2. STK11 and KEAP1 mutations
STK11 and KEAP1 mutations are strongly associated with ICI resistance. These mutations are particularly predictive of resistance in the context of a low TMB. Additionally, co-mutations involving KEAP1 and other genes such as PBRM1, SMARCA4, and TP53 have been shown to correlate with reduced efficacy of immunotherapy, even in cases with high TMB [13,19,20]. These mutations are associated with poor responses to ICIs because of their role in creating an immunosuppressive TME and reducing T cell infiltration [13,21]. In patients with concurrent KRAS mutations, resistance is even more pronounced, with studies showing that these co-mutations correlate with lower overall survival and response rates to ICIs [22–24].
STK11 Mutations: STK11 mutations are associated with poor outcomes with ICIs, especially in the presence of concurrent KRAS mutations. These mutations are associated with a distinct immunophenotype that may contribute to resistance to PD (L) 1 inhibition. Studies have indicated that STK11 mutations create immunosuppressive TME by promoting the infiltration of immunosuppressive cells, such as TAMs and MDSCs, which hinder T-cell activation and proliferation. This immunosuppressive environment is a significant factor in resistance to PD-(L)1 blockade therapies [2,3,6]. The presence of STK11 mutations often correlates with lower TMB, which can further diminish the response to immunotherapy [23,25].
KEAP1 mutations: Similar to STK11, KEAP1 mutations are associated with a poor response to ICIs and lower overall survival, particularly when co-occurring with KRAS mutations, as they are implicated in metabolic reprogramming within the tumor, promoting oxidative stress and creating a hypoxic TME that suppresses immune cell function [3,6]. These mutations can lead to alterations in the TME that reduce immune cell infiltration and activity, contributing to resistance [23,25,26].
Overall, these genetic variations can significantly affect the effectiveness of immunotherapy in older NSCLC patients by influencing TMB and the tumor immune microenvironment. Understanding these genetic factors is crucial for tailoring treatment strategies and improving the outcomes in this patient population. Understanding the combined impact of TMB, specific mutations, and the resulting TME characteristics is crucial for developing tailored treatment strategies. These insights can help refine biomarker-driven approaches to optimize ICIs for improved outcomes in this patient population [3,4,6]. 2.2. Tumor microenvironment
Environmental factors significantly affect the effectiveness of immunotherapy in NSCLC patients through various mechanisms. The immunosuppressive TME, which is characterized by regulatory T cells, low immune cell infiltration, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and tumor-associated macrophages, can hinder the efficacy of ICIs. For instance, TAMs and MDSCs release cytokines and growth factors that suppress T-cell activation, contributing to a local environment that allows tumors to evade immune attacks [2,3]. Metabolic alterations within the TME, such as hypoxia and increased oxidative stress, can also restrict cytotoxic T-cell function by impairing their energy metabolism, reducing their cytolytic activity, and ultimately diminishing the effectiveness of ICIs [8,15,21]. Tumors with low T cell infiltration or an immune-cold phenotype are less likely to respond to ICIs due to this insufficient immune presence, which limits ICIs’ ability to activate an anti-tumor response [5,6,20,27].
This immunosuppressive environment is particularly notable in patients with mutations in STK11, which correlates with less immune cell infiltration and lower PD-L1 expression [24,28]. Additionally, the absence of a “T cell-inflamed” microenvironment is associated with ICI resistance, particularly in NSCLC cases with squamous histology, which are generally less immunogenic than adenocarcinoma [5,8]. A “T cell-inflamed” microenvironment is more common in adenocarcinoma than squamous histology, and its absence can indicate resistance [29].
Factors such as insufficient T cell infiltration, lack of PD-1 expression, deficient interferon signaling, and loss of tumor antigen presentation are critical mechanisms underlying resistance. Elevated levels of plasma cytokines such as TNF, IL-6, and IL-8 are also associated with resistance [12,30]. TME plays a crucial role in modulating responses to ICIs. The presence of immunosuppressive cells, such as regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and tumor-associated macrophages, can create an immunosuppressive environment that reduces the efficacy of ICIs because these cells actively limit immune system activation and T-cell function [31]. Strategies to modify the TME toward a more pro-immunogenic state are being explored to enhance immunotherapy outcomes, including combination therapies that pair ICIs with chemotherapy, radiation, or targeted agents aimed at reducing TAM and MDSC activity, thus enhancing T-cell infiltration and activation [8]. Deficiencies in the antigen presentation pathway, including downregulation of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, can contribute to resistance [27].
Recent evidence suggests that the composition of the gut and respiratory microbiota may directly influence the tumor microenvironment in NSCLC and the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Studies have shown that patients with diverse gut microbiomes tend to respond better to ICIs, likely due to microbiota-driven modulation of systemic immune responses [32]. Certain bacterial genera in the airways are associated with favorable or unfavorable responses to ICIs. Antibiotic use, which disrupts microbiota diversity, has been linked to poor outcomes in patients with NSCLC undergoing immunotherapy [32,33]. Furthermore, the composition of the respiratory microbiota has emerged as a predictor of response, with certain bacterial genera linked to either favorable or unfavorable outcomes in ICI-treated patients [32]. The composition of the respiratory microbiota has been identified as a predictor of response, with certain bacterial genera being associated with either positive or negative outcomes [33].
T-cell exhaustion, a state of dysfunction resulting from chronic antigen exposure, can limit the efficacy of ICIs, even in tumors with high PD-L1 expression and dense immune infiltration. These “inflamed but unresponsive” tumors may display elevated levels of inhibitory receptors (e.g., PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3) on T cells, rendering them functionally impaired despite a favorable immune microenvironment. This underscores the need for better biomarkers beyond PD-L1 and TIL density to predict ICI responses [34].
Additionally, dietary interventions that modulate gut microbiota are being investigated as potential strategies for improving immunotherapy efficacy [32]. These interventions aim to enhance the abundance of beneficial microbial species that support immune functions. Understanding and manipulating these environmental factors, including the TME and microbiota, are critical for optimizing immunotherapy responses in patients with NSCLC.
Younger patients often exhibit a tumor microenvironment with reduced immune system activation, which can contribute to resistance to ICIs. This trend is particularly notable in younger male patients, who have been shown to experience worse survival outcomes with ICIs alone than older male patients, suggesting that immune profile differences related to age may impact treatment efficacy [14]. This is particularly evident in younger male patients, who show worse survival outcomes when treated with immunotherapy alone than older male patients. Conversely, older patients tend to have a more favorable immune microenvironment, which may enhance the efficacy of ICIs [14,35].
In summary, the most relevant biomarkers for predicting resistance to immunotherapy in NSCLC include genetic mutations such as STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR; characteristics of the tumor microenvironment such as immune cell infiltration and cytokine profiles; and the patient’s prior treatment history. Together, these factors provide a comprehensive framework for understanding resistance and can guide therapeutic decision-making, particularly in tailoring combination therapies and biomarker-driven approaches to enhance ICI efficacy [13,19,20,27]. In addition to the tumor burden, systemic metabolic alterations and cancer-associated symptoms in advanced-stage NSCLC contribute to immunotherapy resistance. Cancer cachexia, a multifactorial disorder characterized by muscle wasting and systemic inflammation, is prevalent among patients with metastatic lung cancer and has been linked to poor ICI responses [36]. Chronic inflammation, particularly via the IL-6 and TNF pathways, drives this syndrome and impairs the immune function. Therapeutic interventions targeting inflammation and cachexia pathways may improve ICI efficacy [37].
2.2.1. History of prior treatment
Previous treatments, such as chemotherapy, can alter the TME and immune landscape, potentially affecting subsequent responses to immunotherapy [11]. Patients who have received multiple lines of therapy before starting ICIs are more likely to develop resistance than those treated in the first-line setting. This is particularly true for those who have undergone extensive chemotherapy or targeted therapy, which can alter the TME and immune landscape [12,27]. This is particularly relevant in older patients undergoing extensive prior treatment. Additionally, the sequence of treatments, such as administering tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) after ICIs, can lead to severe toxicity and impact the overall response to immunotherapy [29,38,39].
Bone metastasis at baseline is associated with poor outcomes, prognosis, and resistance to ICIs [27]. Prior treatment history, including extensive therapy and treatment sequence, significantly affects the effectiveness of immunotherapy in older patients with NSCLC, mainly because of their distinct genetic and immune profiles. Older patients often have a higher TMB and favorable immune microenvironment that can enhance ICI efficacy [14]. However, the sequence and extent of the prior treatment can alter these benefits.
Chemotherapy: Prior chemotherapy is associated with reduced response to ICIs and worse overall survival. This is likely due to chemotherapy-induced changes in the tumor microenvironment and immune system, such as reduced immune cell infiltration and altered cytokine profiles [40].
Antibiotics: Although not statistically significant, prior antibiotic use may negatively impact ICI response by disrupting the gut microbiome, which modulates immune responses [40].
Radiation Therapy: Previous thoracic radiation therapy has been shown to improve the efficacy of ICIs, potentially owing to enhanced antigen presentation and immune activation. In contrast, extra-thoracic radiation may lead to inferior outcomes [41].
Combination Therapy: In older adults, combining ICIs with chemotherapy does not significantly improve survival compared with ICIs alone and increases the risk of severe adverse events. This suggests that ICI monotherapy may be preferable for this demographic, especially for patients with PD-L1-positive tumors [42].
Overall, the impact of prior treatments on immunotherapy effectiveness in older NSCLC patients is multifaceted, involving interactions between treatment-induced changes and patients’ genetic and immune profiles. These factors should be considered carefully when designing treatment strategies for this population.

2.2.2. Age-related factors
Age-related factors significantly influence immunotherapy resistance in patients with NSCLC, with variations in genetic mutations, tumor microenvironment characteristics, prior treatment history, and patient demographics.
Age and sex are critical demographic factors influencing resistance. Immunosenescence, or aging of the immune system, can reduce the effectiveness of ICIs in older patients by impairing immune cell function and altering cytokine profiles [11]. Younger patients, especially males, show distinct genomic and immune profiles that contribute to resistance. In contrast, older patients generally have a higher TMB and a more immunogenic tumor microenvironment, which can improve their responses to ICIs. Furthermore, female patients are more likely to develop primary resistance to ICIs, which may be influenced by both genetic and immune factors [14,35,38].
In summary, age-related factors, including genetic mutations, tumor microenvironment characteristics, prior treatment history, and patient demographics, significantly influence immunotherapy resistance in NSCLC patients. These factors should be carefully considered when developing personalized treatment strategies to overcome drug resistance and improve patient outcomes. 3. Discussion
Despite significant advances in immunotherapy, resistance to ICIs in NSCLC remains a major obstacle that limits the long-term benefits for many patients. Both intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms are driven by a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and treatment-related factors, such as mutations in genes like STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR, which contribute to an immunosuppressive TME that impedes T-cell infiltration and activation [16]. Overcoming these barriers requires a comprehensive approach incorporating multiple strategies to counteract resistance at various levels. Advances in understanding the TME, genetic mutations, and patient-specific factors such as tumor mutational burden (TMB) and cytokine profiles have paved the way for innovative approaches to improve immunotherapy outcomes [4,6].
This discussion highlights critical strategies for addressing resistance, including combination therapies that enhance immune cell infiltration and antigen presentation, dual checkpoint inhibition to target multiple immunosuppressive pathways, and biomarker-driven approaches to identifying patients most likely to benefit from ICIs [5,8]. By targeting resistance mechanisms through these diverse methods, there is potential to expand the benefits of ICIs and personalize treatment options for patients with NSCLC facing therapeutic challenges. 4. Strategies to overcome resistance
Overcoming resistance to immunotherapy in NSCLC involves several strategies, primarily focusing on combination therapies, biomarker-driven approaches, and targeting of various mechanisms within the TME. These strategies, informed by a deeper understanding of resistance mechanisms, promise to improve the outcomes of NSCLC patients undergoing immunotherapy.
4.1. Combination therapies
Combining ICIs with chemotherapy, targeted therapies, or anti-angiogenic agents can enhance the efficacy by modulating the TME and improving immune cell infiltration [1,30]. For example, chemotherapy can increase the release of tumor antigens, making the tumor more visible to the immune system. In addition, anti-angiogenic agents can normalize tumor blood vessels and improve immune cell access to cancer cells [8]. The combination of ICIs with additional immunotherapies, such as bispecific antibodies, neoantigen vaccines, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, has also been explored to potentiate antitumor responses. For instance, combining anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies with CTLA-4 inhibitors or targeting novel immune checkpoints like TIGIT, LAG-3, and TIM-3 can further enhance immune responses and overcome resistance mechanisms [5,30,43].
4.2. Dual immune checkpoint blockade
Targeting multiple immune checkpoints simultaneously has shown promise for overcoming resistance. For example, combining PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors with CTLA-4 inhibitors can enhance T-cell activity and immune responses by blocking the inhibitory pathways that tumors exploit to evade detection [44,45]. Multiple studies have explored the effectiveness of combining anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 antibodies in the treatment of lung cancer. A phase 1b study showed that the combination of durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) and tremelimumab (anti-CTLA-4) had clinical activity in both PD-L1 positive and negative patients with advanced NSCLC, achieving a 23% confirmed ORR [45,46]. This approach aims to block multiple inhibitory pathways that tumors exploit to evade immune detection [5].
4.3. Modulation of the TME
TME plays a crucial role in resistance to immunotherapy. Strategies to modulate the TME include targeting regulatory T cells (Tregs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and altering the cytokine environment. For example, combining ICIs with anti-angiogenic agents or metabolic modulators, such as IDO-1 inhibitors, can reprogram the TME to be more conducive to immune attack [1,16].
4.4. Novel immunotherapeutic targets
Emerging targets, such as the RIG-I and STING pathways, are being investigated for their potential to enhance anti-tumor immunity. These pathways activate innate immune responses that promote T-cell priming and immune memory, thereby enhancing the efficacy of ICIs [1]. For example, STING agonists can stimulate the release of type I interferons, which improve antigen presentation and T-cell recruitment [1]. Additional strategies include modulating the tumor microenvironment, targeting T cell priming, and using personalized cancer vaccines. These approaches aim to enhance the efficacy of ICIs and delay or prevent drug resistance [43,47].
4.5. Engineered cytokine therapies
Combining cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-2, which can potentiate T cell responses, has shown potential. However, toxicity associated with high doses of these cytokines may be a limitation. Recent studies have developed nontoxic variants and modified cytokines with targeted delivery to enhance their therapeutic index while minimizing systemic side effects, making them more viable ICI adjuvants [48].
4.6. Biomarker-driven approaches
Identifying biomarkers that predict the response to ICIs can help tailor therapies for individual patients. This includes assessing PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and other molecular signatures that indicate susceptibility to specific immunotherapeutic strategies [11]. Combinatorial biomarker strategies, such as considering TMB in conjunction with specific genetic alterations (e.g., STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR), can help tailor immunotherapy and limit overtreatment. Biomarkers, such as plasma cytokine levels (TNF, IL-6, and IL-8), can also guide treatment decisions and predict resistance [12,13]. In addition to genetic mutations such as STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR, several other biomarkers should be monitored to comprehensively assess resistance to immunotherapy in NSCLC.
Recent advancements in nanoplasmonic biosensors, particularly surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) technologies, offer promising avenues for sensitive and noninvasive cancer biomarker detection. Technologies such as Inverse Molecular Sentinel (iMS) biosensors enable real-time, point-of-care diagnostics by identifying nucleotide biomarkers linked to various cancers [49]. Given the challenge of resistance in NSCLC, these biosensors could play a pivotal role in monitoring treatment responses and detecting early signs of resistance, allowing timely therapeutic adjustments to improve patient outcomes.
4.7. Additional biomarkers and predictors
Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB): High TMB is associated with better responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors, whereas low TMB can indicate resistance, especially for specific genetic mutations [13].
Microsatellite Instability (MSI): While MSI-high status is uncommon in NSCLC, it can predict positive responses to ICIs [50].
PD-L1 Expression: While PD-L1 expression remains a key biomarker for predicting response to ICIs. However, its predictive value can vary and should be considered along with other factors [51,52].
Antigen Presentation Pathway: Alterations in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and β2-microglobulin can affect antigen presentation and contribute to resistance [50].
Immune Cell Infiltration and T-cell Receptor (TCR) Clonality: The presence and diversity of T-cell populations within the tumor microenvironment are crucial for effective immune responses [53,54].
Cytokine Profiles: Elevated levels of cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 can indicate an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [27].
Gut Microbiome: Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiome may influence the efficacy of immunotherapy, although this is still under investigation [51].
Chromatin Remodeling Genes: Alterations in genes such as ARID1A, PBRM1, and SMARCA4 are associated with resistance and should be considered in genomic profiling [50].
In summary, addressing immunotherapy resistance in NSCLC requires a multifaceted approach that combines combination therapies, biomarker-driven strategies, and targeted modifications of the TME. The integration of ICIs with complementary therapies and the identification of predictive biomarkers such as TMB, PD-L1 expression, and genetic mutations such as STK11 and KEAP1 hold promise for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and tailoring treatments to individual patient profiles. Advances in the understanding of novel pathways and leveraging insights from the gut microbiome and cytokine profiles further broaden the potential for overcoming resistance.
As research continues to uncover complex resistance mechanisms, a personalized approach that combines robust biomarker assessment and innovative therapeutic strategies will be essential for optimizing the outcomes of NSCLC patients facing immunotherapy challenges. This comprehensive approach improves treatment precision and paves the way for future advances in the management of resistant NSCLC. When evaluated together, these biomarkers can provide a more thorough understanding of the potential resistance mechanisms and guide personalized treatment strategies for NSCLC.
5. Conclusion
Addressing immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) requires a multifaceted approach that integrates combination therapies, biomarker-guided strategies, modulation of the tumor microenvironment, and the exploration of new therapeutic targets. A comprehensive understanding of patient-specific resistance mechanisms can improve treatment outcomes and optimize therapeutic choices. Key strategies for enhancing immunotherapy efficacy include dual checkpoint blockade, targeted TME modulation, engineered cytokine therapies, and innovative diagnostic technologies, such as SERS biosensors, which facilitate timely and precise treatment adjustments.
By leveraging insights from biomarkers and novel therapeutic combinations, personalized treatment plans can be developed to reduce resistance and improve outcomes in patients with NSCLC.
6. Future perspective
Over the next 5–10 years, the landscape of immunotherapy for NSCLC is expected to shift toward more personalized and biomarker-driven strategies. Integrative profiling of genetic alterations, immune context, and patient-specific factors, including age, prior treatments, and microbiota composition, will be key to refining patient selection for immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Emerging technologies, such as single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and artificial intelligence, are likely to uncover new predictive signatures and resistance pathways. Moreover, targeting the tumor microenvironment through agents modulating myeloid cells, fibroblasts, or inflammatory mediators will expand beyond PD-1/PD-L1 inhibition alone. In parallel, geriatric oncology will gain prominence, with more trials focusing on elderly and frail populations that have historically been underrepresented. Combination strategies involving ICIs, metabolic modulators, vaccines, and microbiome therapies may redefine the standard of care. Ultimately, overcoming immunotherapy resistance will require multidisciplinary longitudinal approaches that integrate molecular diagnostics, host biology, and dynamic treatment adaptation.

Article highlights
Immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is multifactorial and involves genetic, environmental, and host-related variables.
This review presents an integrative framework that includes tumor genetics, tumor microenvironment, prior treatment history, and age-related immune dysfunction.
Specific genomic alterations (e.g. STK11, KEAP1, and EGFR) and immune-excluded phenotypes have been linked to reduced ICI efficacy.
Treatment history (chemotherapy and radiotherapy) and systemic inflammation (e.g. cancer-related cachexia) modulate immune response and influence resistance.
Older patients present with unique immune characteristics that may enhance or impair ICI responses, underscoring the need for age-specific therapeutic approaches.
Future strategies should combine ICIs with agents targeting the microenvironment, metabolism, or microbiota guided by multidimensional biomarker profiles.
